section.h2: Frequently Asked Questions About FLOT vs SOX vs CAPOX Perioperative Chemotherapy for Resectable Gastric Cancer
section.intro: FLOT, SOX, and CAPOX are chemotherapy regimens used around surgery for resectable gastric cancer. This guide explains how they differ, who they may suit, and what patients and caregivers commonly ask.

items.q: What is FLOT chemotherapy for gastric cancer?
items.a: FLOT is a four-drug chemotherapy regimen combining fluorouracil, leucovorin, oxaliplatin, and docetaxel, given around surgery for resectable gastric or gastro-oesophageal junction cancer. It is usually delivered every two weeks, with several cycles before surgery and several after. FLOT is often considered for fitter patients because the added docetaxel can increase intensity. Suitability depends on cancer stage, overall health, and specialist review, and should be discussed with a qualified oncology team.

items.q: What are SOX and CAPOX chemotherapy?
items.a: SOX and CAPOX are two-drug chemotherapy regimens that pair oxaliplatin with an oral fluoropyrimidine. SOX uses S-1, while CAPOX uses capecitabine, both taken as tablets alongside intravenous oxaliplatin. These regimens are widely used for gastric cancer, often on a three-week cycle. Because they involve oral drugs and fewer agents than FLOT, they may be considered for selected patients where convenience or tolerability matters, based on specialist assessment.

Perioperative chemotherapy means chemotherapy given both before and after surgery for resectable cancer. The pre-surgery (neoadjuvant) part aims to shrink the tumour and treat hidden microscopic spread, while the post-surgery (adjuvant) part targets any remaining cancer cells. This approach is a standard strategy for many gastric cancers. Whether a patient completes both phases depends on response, recovery, tolerance, and decisions made by the treating medical team.

items.q: How do FLOT, SOX, and CAPOX differ?
items.a: The main difference is the number and type of drugs. FLOT uses four agents including docetaxel and is typically more intensive, while SOX and CAPOX are two-drug oxaliplatin-based regimens using oral S-1 or capecitabine. FLOT is given every two weeks; SOX and CAPOX usually every three weeks. Choice depends on cancer type, stage, patient fitness, side-effect profile, and regional practice, and should be decided by the treating oncology team.

items.q: Who is eligible for FLOT chemotherapy?
items.a: FLOT may be suitable for selected patients with resectable gastric or gastro-oesophageal junction cancer who are fit enough for a more intensive four-drug regimen. Doctors typically assess age, performance status, organ function, and other health conditions before recommending it. Because docetaxel adds intensity, FLOT is not appropriate for everyone. Final eligibility depends on cancer stage, overall health, and specialist review, and should be confirmed by the treating oncology team.

items.q: When might SOX or CAPOX be preferred over FLOT?
items.a: SOX or CAPOX may be preferred when a less intensive, oxaliplatin-based regimen is a better fit for the patient. This can include older patients, those with reduced fitness, or people who may tolerate two drugs better than four. The oral fluoropyrimidine can also reduce hospital visits. These are general considerations only; the choice depends on cancer type, stage, health, and specialist judgement, and should be discussed with the treating team.

items.q: How is perioperative chemotherapy given around surgery?
items.a: Perioperative chemotherapy is usually given in cycles before surgery, followed by a recovery period, then surgery, and further cycles afterward. FLOT is commonly given every two weeks, while SOX and CAPOX use three-week cycles, with oral tablets taken at home and oxaliplatin given by drip. The exact schedule, number of cycles, and timing of surgery depend on response and tolerance, as decided by the treating medical team.

items.q: What are the common side effects of these regimens?
items.a: Common side effects include nausea, fatigue, low blood counts, diarrhoea, and oxaliplatin-related nerve tingling in the hands and feet. FLOT may add a higher risk of low white cells, hair loss, and infection because of docetaxel, while capecitabine and S-1 can cause hand-foot skin changes. Side effects vary between patients and regimens. Supportive care can help, and any symptoms should be reported to the treating oncology team promptly.

items.q: How much does FLOT, SOX, or CAPOX chemotherapy cost?
items.a: Costs vary widely depending on the regimen, country, hospital, and number of cycles. Two-drug regimens like SOX and CAPOX are often less expensive than four-drug FLOT, partly because of oral tablets and fewer supportive medications. Additional costs may include tests, day-care fees, and management of side effects. Final cost depends on hospital, diagnosis, stage, protocol, complications, length of stay, and treating team advice, so estimates should be confirmed locally.

items.q: Are FLOT, SOX, and CAPOX available in India?
items.a: FLOT, SOX, and CAPOX are used at many cancer centres in India for resectable gastric cancer, subject to specialist assessment. The generic availability of drugs such as oxaliplatin, capecitabine, docetaxel, and fluorouracil can make these regimens more accessible in some settings. Availability of a specific regimen still depends on the hospital, drug supply, and clinical suitability, and treatment decisions should always be made by the treating oncology team.

items.q: Which countries commonly use SOX and CAPOX?
items.a: SOX and CAPOX are widely used across Asia, including China, Japan, and South Korea, where oral fluoropyrimidines such as S-1 have been extensively studied for gastric cancer. CAPOX is also commonly used in Europe and other regions. FLOT is frequently used in Europe and North America for fitter patients. Regional practice, drug availability, and clinical guidelines influence which regimen is offered, and choices should be confirmed with the treating team.

items.q: Does the cost differ between China, India, and the USA?
items.a: Treatment costs for these regimens generally differ across countries, with India and China often lower than the USA for chemotherapy and hospital care. However, total cost depends on the specific regimen, number of cycles, tests, surgery, hospital category, and any complications. Cross-country comparisons are only estimates and can change over time. Patients should request a written, itemised estimate from each hospital and confirm details with the treating medical team.

items.q: Is immunotherapy ever added to these chemotherapy regimens?
items.a: In some situations, immunotherapy such as a PD-1 inhibitor may be combined with chemotherapy, but this is usually guided by biomarkers like PD-L1 and by tumour characteristics. For resectable gastric cancer, adding immunotherapy to perioperative chemotherapy is an area of active research and evolving practice rather than a universal standard. Whether it may be considered depends on biomarker profile, stage, and specialist review, and should be discussed with the treating oncology team.

items.q: Are there clinical trials comparing FLOT, SOX, and CAPOX?
items.a: Yes, clinical trials have compared and continue to study these regimens, including how they perform with or without added agents such as immunotherapy. Trial participation may offer access to newer approaches under close monitoring, but eligibility is decided only after medical record review and investigator assessment. Trials often have strict inclusion and exclusion criteria, and enrolment or benefit cannot be guaranteed. Interested patients should discuss suitable options with their oncology team.

items.q: What happens if chemotherapy does not shrink the tumour before surgery?
items.a: If pre-surgery chemotherapy does not shrink the tumour as hoped, the treating team may reassess the plan using repeat imaging and clinical review. Options can include changing the regimen, proceeding to surgery if the cancer remains resectable, or considering other treatments or trials. Response varies between patients and cannot be predicted in advance. Any change in approach should be based on scans, overall health, and decisions made by the treating oncology team.

items.q: What reports are needed to plan perioperative chemotherapy abroad?
items.a: Planning treatment abroad usually requires recent imaging (such as CT or PET-CT), the endoscopy and biopsy report, pathology confirming gastric cancer, and relevant biomarker results like HER2 and PD-L1 where available. Blood tests and a summary of previous treatment also help specialists assess suitability. Requirements vary by hospital. Access abroad depends on hospital acceptance, medical review, visa approval, and travel fitness, and final decisions rest with the treating medical team.

items.q: Can chemotherapy be started in one country and continued in another?
items.a: In some cases perioperative chemotherapy may be started in one country and continued in another, but this requires careful coordination between medical teams. Clear records of the exact regimen, doses, cycle dates, and side effects are essential so care can continue safely. Continuity also depends on drug availability and hospital acceptance. This should be planned in advance with both treating teams, and final decisions must be made by the qualified oncology team.

items.q: How does CancerFax help patients with FLOT vs SOX vs CAPOX chemotherapy?
items.a: CancerFax helps patients organize medical reports, identify relevant specialists or treatment centers, estimate possible costs, and coordinate second opinions, appointments, travel, visa, and follow-up support. Treatment decisions about FLOT, SOX, or CAPOX are always made by the qualified oncology team after reviewing the patient's diagnosis, stage, biomarkers, previous treatment, and overall health. This support is intended to assist patients and caregivers, not to replace medical advice from the treating team.
